what: Reading all images into memory using lapply()
title: Analyzing multiple images at once
text: example , ’ll use base R’s lapply() function read images. However, can course use purrr::map() just well. Using lapply() simple: tell R apply img_read() function every element fileNames object. result list every list element contains image matrix. Thus, object might big! code works perfectly fine every image can read without problems (usually case). However, want robust version, can also define custom img_read() function includes error handling tryCatch.
code: # read all images at once into memory allImages <- lapply(fileNames, img_read) # define custom image read function that catches errors and returns NA img_read_no_error <- function(img) {   tryCatch(img_read(img), error=function(e) NA) }  # read images with custom function allImages <- lapply(fileNames, img_read_no_error)

what: Computing image fluency scores using lapply()
title: Analyzing multiple images at once
text: images read memory, can compute image fluency scores images. facilitate process contrast, self-similarity, simplicity, symmetry, define function computes scores given image, apply function images. ’s done, can convert results data frame add images’ file names. final step, add typicality scores previous section look results.
code: # define function that computes all image fluency scores except typicality img_fluency_scores <- function(img) {   contr <- tryCatch(img_contrast(img), error = function(e) NA)   selfsim <- tryCatch(img_self_similarity(img), error = function(e) NA)   simpl <- tryCatch(img_simplicity(img), error = function(e) NA)   sym <- tryCatch(img_symmetry(img, horizontal = FALSE), error = function(e) NA)   return(c(contrast = contr,                self_similarity = selfsim,               simplicity = simpl,               symmetry = unname(sym))) }  # apply function to images results <- lapply(allImages, img_fluency_scores) # convert results to data frame and add file names results <- do.call(rbind, results) results <- data.frame(filename = basename(fileNames), results) # compute and add typicality to results results$typicality <- as.vector(img_typicality(allImages))  # print a nicely formatted results table knitr::kable(results, digits = 3)

title: Analyzing multiple images at once
text: code using lapply() faster approach using first big loop reading images compute typicality. However, might gain much larger increase speed using parallelized versions lapply() purrr::map(), respectively. following code example briefly demonstrates achieve . Essentially, replace instances lapply() parallel::mclapply() (multi-core lapply). example , however, ’ll use pbmcapply::pbmclapply adds progress bar (pb) multi-core lapply. Let’s quick comparison computing time computing four image fluency scores without multi-core processing. Note increasing file size number images, speed-become larger. ‘simulate’ reading images 10 times. can see multi-core approach  three times faster (single test run) single-core approach! Let’s see furrr::future_map() compares . Finally, confirm results .
code: # detect cores for multi-core processing ncores <- parallel::detectCores()  # read images with multi-core lapply and progress bar allImages <- pbmcapply::pbmclapply(fileNames, img_read_no_error, mc.cores = ncores)  # compute image fluency scores  results <- pbmcapply::pbmclapply(allImages, img_fluency_scores, mc.cores = ncores)  # convert results to data frame and add file names results <- do.call(rbind, results) results <- data.frame(filename = basename(fileNames), results)  # compute and add typicality to results results$typicality <- as.vector(img_typicality(allImages)) # read images 10 times  allImages <- lapply(rep(fileNames, 10), img_read_no_error) cat('Number of images:', length(allImages), '\n') > Number of images: 110 # compute imagefluency scores using lapply() with progress bar tictoc::tic("lapply") results_lapply <- pbapply::pblapply(allImages, img_fluency_scores) tictoc::toc(log=TRUE) > lapply: 8.73 sec elapsed # compute imagefluency scores using multi-core lapply() with progress bar tictoc::tic("pbmclapply") results_pbmclapply <- pbmcapply::pbmclapply(allImages, img_fluency_scores,                                             mc.cores = ncores) tictoc::toc(log=TRUE) > pbmclapply: 2.44 sec elapsed library(dplyr) future::plan('multisession')  tictoc::tic('future_map') results_future_map <- allImages %>% furrr::future_map(img_fluency_scores,                                       .progress = TRUE,                                       .options = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE)) tictoc::toc(log=TRUE) > future_map: 2.98 sec elapsed all.equal(results_lapply, results_pbmclapply) > [1] TRUE all.equal(results_lapply, results_future_map) > [1] TRUE

what: Motivation: Why create yet another R package
title: Getting started
text: last decades, amount data generated growing rapidly, predominantly due digitalization. today’s data unstructured, share increasing. Given unstructured data rich, data provide rich insights scientific research variety fields practice alike. Especially images (.e., visual stimuli) recognized valuable source information. time, vision research research psychology show even simple changes low-level image features (like symmetry, contrast, complexity) can tremendous effect variety human judgments. example, statement like “Nut bread healthier potato bread” likely perceived true presented color easy read white background (high contrast) instead presented color difficult read white background (low contrast; cf. [1]). Thus, might useful estimate control differences low-level visual features research includes visual stimuli. imagefluency R package low-level image scores based processing fluency theory. package provides scores several basic aesthetic principles facilitate fluent cognitive processing images: contrast, complexity / simplicity, self-similarity, symmetry, typicality.

what: Why and when to use the package
title: Getting started
text: Possible applications include: stimulus selection experiments (e.g., testing brand logos, evaluating product designs, online display ads) control variables statistical prediction models linking image fluency scores outcomes interest (e.g., typical product packaging look like, simpler images get less attention website, …) (interpretable) image features simple machine learning models, e.g. SVM image classifier

title: Getting started
text: prevailing explanation low-level image features affect human judgments based processing fluency theory [2]. Processing fluency describes ease processing stimulus [3], happens instantaneously automatically [4]. Higher processing fluency results gut-level positive affective response [5]. Notably, rich body literature shown processing fluency effects impact variety judgmental domains everyday life, including much like things, much consider statements true, trustworthy judge person, risky think something , whether buy product (review, see [6]). Several stimulus features proposed result increased fluency. particular, visual symmetry, simplicity, (proto-)typicality, contrast identified facilitate processing [2]. Recent studies discuss self-similarity light fluency-based aesthetics [7, 8], concept studied example images natural scenes [9]. Self-similarity can described self-repeating patterns within stimulus. typical example leaves ferns feature shape regardless magnification reduction (.e., scale invariance). Another prominent example romanesco broccoli self-similar surface. Extracting image features contrast, self-similarity, simplicity, symmetry, typicality therefore constitutes core purpose imagefluency package.

title: Getting started
text: function img_contrast() returns contrast image. research defines contrast images root-mean-squared (RMS) contrast, standard deviation normalized pixel intensity values [10]: 1MN∑=0N−1∑j=0M−1(Iij−‾)2\sqrt{\frac{1}{M N}\sum_{=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=0}^{M - 1}(I_{ij} - \bar{})^2}. RMS image measure visual contrast shown predict human contrast detection thresholds well [11]. Therefore, function calculates contrast computing RMS contrast input image. Consequently, higher value indicates higher contrast. image normalized necessary (.e., normalization range [0, 1]). color images, weighted average color channels computed (cf. [8]). Note following, example images come package used. Moreover, images can displayed using grid.raster() function grid package. Calculating contrast scores two images gives following result: score: 0.08 score: 0.29
code: # Example image with relatively high contrast: berries berries <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'berries.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(berries) # get contrast img_contrast(berries) # Example image with relatively low contrast: bike bike <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'bike.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(bike) # get contrast img_contrast(bike)

title: Getting started
text: function img_complexity() returns visual complexity image. Algorithmic information theory indicates picture complexity can measured accurately image compression rates complex images denser fewer redundancies [12, 13]. Therefore, function calculates visual complexity image ratio compressed uncompressed image file size. Thus, value depend image size. function takes file path image file (URL) pre-loaded image input argument returns ratio compressed divided uncompressed image file size. complexity values naturally interpretable can range almost 0 (virtually completely compressed image, thus extremely simple image) 1 (compression possible, thus extremely complex image). function offers use different image compression algorithms like jpg, gif, png algorithm = 'zip' default (discussion different algorithms, see [8]). compression algorithms depict horizontal vertical redundancies equally, function includes optional rotate parameter (default: FALSE). Setting parameter TRUE additionally creates compressed version rotated image. overall compressed image’s file size computed minimum original image’s file size file size rotated image. function img_simplicity() returns visual simplicity image. Image simplicity complement image complexity therefore calculated 1 minus complexity score (.e., compression rate). Values can range 0 (compression possible, thus extremely complex image) almost 1 (virtually completely compressed image, thus extremely simple image). Calculating complexity scores two images gives following result: score: 0.90 score: 0.42
code: # Example image with high complexity: trees trees <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'trees.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(trees) # get complexity img_complexity(trees) # Example image with low complexity: sky sky <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'sky.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(sky) # get complexity img_complexity(sky)

title: Getting started
text: function img_self_similarity() returns self-similarity image. Self-similarity can measured Fourier power spectrum image. Previous research identified spectral power natural scenes falls spatial frequencies (ff) according power law (1fp\frac{1}{f^p}) values pp near value 2, indicates scale invariance (review, see [14]). Therefore, function computes self-similarity via slope log-log power spectrum image using OLS. value self-similarity returned function calculated self-similarity=|slope+2|*(−1)\text{self-similarity} = |\text{slope} + 2| * (-1). , measure reaches maximum value 0 slope −2-2, deviation −2-2 results negative values negative higher deviation −2-2. Thus, range self-similarity scores −∞-\infty 00. color images, weighted average color channel’s values computed. possible get raw regression slope (instead transformed value indicates self-similarity) using option raw = TRUE. options include possibility plot log-log power spectrum (logplot = TRUE) base computation slope full frequency spectrum (full = TRUE). Images square default resized square power spectrum computed; resize = FALSE, power spectrum computed original image without resizing. See function’s help file details (.e., ?img_self_similarity). Calculating self-similarity scores two images gives result . score romanesco broccoli much closer maximum possible value 0, hence much self-similar. score: -0.03 score: -1.22
code: # Example image with high self-similarity: romanesco romanesco <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'romanesco.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(romanesco) # get self-similarity img_self_similarity(romanesco) # Example image with low self-similarity: office office <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'office.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(office) # get self-similarity img_self_similarity(office)

title: Getting started
text: function img_symmetry() returns vertical horizontal symmetry image numeric value 0 (symmetrical) 1 (perfectly symmetrical). Symmetry computed correlation corresponding image halves (.e., pairwise correlation corresponding pixels, cf. [15]). perceptual mirror axis necessarily exactly middle picture, function detects first step ‘optimal’ mirror axis estimating several symmetry values different positions mirror axis. end, 5% image width cut left right side image (case vertical symmetry; analogously horizontal symmetry), shifts mirror axis (.e., middle remaining image part) 2.5% image width right left. second step, overall symmetry score computed maximum symmetry scores given different mirror axes. color images, weighted average color channel’s values computed. See [8] details. function two optional logical parameters: vertical horizontal (TRUE default). one parameters set FALSE, vertical horizontal symmetry computed, respectively. See function’s help file (.e., ?img_symmetry) information additional options shift_range per_channel. speed computation, best position mirror axis located fast Fourier transform, symmetry score position computed directly correlation image halves. option exact = TRUE, correlation instead computed directly every position mirror axis. considerably slower rarely leads (minimally) different result (see function’s help file). Calculating vertical symmetry scores two images gives following result: score: 0.96 score: 0.48
code: # Example image with high vertical symmetry: rails rails <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'rails.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(rails) # get only vertical symmetry img_symmetry(rails, horizontal = FALSE) # Example image with low vertical symmetry: bridge bridge <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'bridge.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) # display image grid::grid.raster(bridge) # get only vertical symmetry img_symmetry(bridge, horizontal = FALSE)

title: Getting started
text: function img_typicality() returns visual typicality set images relative . Values can range -1 (inversely typical) 0 (typical) 1 (perfectly typical). , higher absolute values indicate larger typicality. typicality score computed correlation particular image average representation images, .e., mean images [16]. , typicality image assessed isolation, comparison set images category. color images, weighted average color channel’s values computed. images different dimensions automatically resized smallest height width. Rescaling images prior computing typicality scores can specified optional rescaling parameter (must numeric value). rescaling possible assess typicality different perceptual levels (see [17] details). users won’t need rescaling can use default (rescale = NULL). following example shows three images two depict valleys mountains one depicts fireworks. Therefore, fireworks image comparison rather low typicality set images (.e., atypical). important note image’s typicality score highly depends reference set image compared. Calculating typicality scores three images gives following result: score: 0.75 score: 0.40 score: 0.72
code: # Example images depicting valleys: valley_white, valley_green # Example image depicting fireworks: fireworks valley_white <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'valley_white.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) valley_green <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'valley_green.jpg', package = 'imagefluency')) fireworks <- img_read(system.file('example_images', 'fireworks.jpg', package = 'imagefluency'))  # create image set as list imglist <- list(valley_white, fireworks, valley_green)  # get typicality img_typicality(imglist)

title: Image self-similarity — img_self_similarity
text: function takes (square) array matrix numeric integer   values representing image input returns self-similarity   image. Self-similarity computed via slope log-log power   spectrum using OLS. slope near -2 indicates fractal-like   properties (see Redies et al., 2007; Simoncelli & Olshausen, 2001). Thus,   value self-similarity returned function   calculated self-similarity = abs(slope + 2) * (-1). , measure   reaches maximum value 0 slope -2, deviation -2   results negative values negative higher deviation   -2. color images, weighted average color channel's   values computed (cf. Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). default, frequency range 10 256 cycles per image   used interpolation. Computation full range can set via   parameter full = TRUE. Note highest frequency image   half (smaller) side length pixels. small images, slope   therefore estimated frequencies (e.g.,   frequencies 10 11 image 22 pixels). function throws   warning slope estimated fewer 10 frequencies (.e.,   images side length less 38 pixels full = FALSE). Self-similarity computed image without variation   (e.g., image one color; color images, applies   color channel). case, function returns NA   throws warning. logplot set TRUE log-log plot power   spectrum additionally shown. package ggplot2 installed   plot includes slope OLS regression. Note option   currently implemented grayscale images. possible get raw regression slope (instead transformed   value indicates self-similarity) using option raw =   TRUE. power spectrum computed square image. default, image   square therefore first resized square (bilinear   resizing longer image side length shorter side,   complete image content kept). Note, however,   interpolation smooths image: fine details attenuated strongly   coarse structures, makes slope power spectrum   steeper. size effect depends image size   aspect ratio, larger small images. resize =   FALSE, image resized. Instead, power spectrum computed   complete, original image, spatial frequencies (  cycles per image, horizontal vertical direction)   resized image contain analyzed. also uses complete   image content avoids smoothing. square images, resize   effect.

text: function returns vertical horizontal mirror symmetry   image img. Symmetry values can range 0 (symmetrical)   1 (fully symmetrical). vertical horizontal set   FALSE vertical horizontal symmetry computed,   respectively. perceptual mirror axis necessarily exactly middle   picture, function estimates first step several symmetry values   different positions mirror axis. end, 5%   (default) image width cut left right side   image (case vertical symmetry; analogously horizontal   symmetry), symmetry remaining image part computed.   mirror axis always middle remaining image part, cutting   5% image width shifts mirror axis 2.5%   image width right left. second step, overall   symmetry score computed maximum symmetry scores given   different mirror axes. See Mayer & Landwehr (2018) details. Advanced users can change shift range optional parameter   shift_range, takes numeric decimal 0 1   input (maximum share image width cut ). default   shift_range = 0.05 (.e., 5%). Symmetry computed one image halves variation   (e.g., image half one color; color images,   applies color channel). case, function returns   NA respective symmetry throws warning. color   images color channel variation (e.g., image   consists black red), consider converting image   grayscale first (see rgb2gray). color images, default first maximal symmetry score (  explained ) obtained per color channel (parameter per_channel   = TRUE). Subsequently, weighted average color channel's   maximal score computed image's overall symmetry. Advanced users   can reverse order setting per_channel = FALSE. results   first computing weighted averages position mirror   axis separately, afterwards finding maximal overall symmetry score. keep computation fast, best position mirror axis   located fast Fourier transform (FFT), yields symmetry   values positions mirror axis . symmetry score   best position computed directly correlation   two image halves. result   correlation computed directly every position mirror axis,   unless symmetry values two positions practically tied   (difference smaller 1e-10). rare case, score might   differ correspondingly small amount. Setting exact = TRUE   computes correlation directly every position mirror axis   (method used version 1.0.1), avoids expense   speed (computation takes several times longer; large images,   ten times longer). perfectly symmetric image (.e., two image halves identical   mirror images ) always receives score exactly 1.

title: RGB to Gray Conversion — rgb2gray
text: matrix grayscale values.

title: RGB to Gray Conversion — rgb2gray
text: function takes 3-dimensional array   numeric integer values input (img)   returns matrix grayscale values output.   grayscale values computed GRAY = 0.299 *   RED + 0.587 * GREEN + 0.114 * BLUE (recommended   ITU-R BT.601). array fourth dimension   (.e., alpha channel), fourth dimension ignored.

title: RGB to Gray Conversion — rgb2gray
code: # construct a sample RGB image as array of random integers imgRed <- matrix(runif(100, min = 0, max = 255), 10, 10) imgGreen <- matrix(runif(100, min = 0, max = 255), 10, 10) imgBlue <- matrix(runif(100, min = 0, max = 255), 10, 10) imgColor <- array(c(imgRed, imgGreen, imgBlue), dim = c(10, 10, 3))  # convert to gray img <- rgb2gray(imgColor)

title: Matrix or Array Rotation by 90 Degrees — rotate90
text: function takes array matrix input   object (img) returns object rotated   90 degrees. default, rotation done   mathematically positive direction (.e.,   counterclockwise). Clockwise rotation (.e.,   mathematically negative) can specified passing   value "negative" direction   argument.

title: Matrix or Array Rotation by 90 Degrees — rotate90
code: # sample matrix img <- matrix(1:6, ncol = 2) img #>      [,1] [,2] #> [1,]    1    4 #> [2,]    2    5 #> [3,]    3    6  rotate90(img) # counterclockwise #>      [,1] [,2] [,3] #> [1,]    4    5    6 #> [2,]    1    2    3 rotate90(img, direction = "negative") # clockwise #>      [,1] [,2] [,3] #> [1,]    3    2    1 #> [2,]    6    5    4
